negotiated by the Cigar Makers Inter-
national Union of America with the
Cigar Manufacturers Association of
Tampa is another outstanding achieve
ment of bona fide trade union organ
ization based upon collective bargain
ing and other principles applied by the i.
national and international unions af-
filiated with the American Federation
of Labor.


The contract, covering members of
Local Unions Nos. 1886, 462, 474, 493,
494, 495, 500, and any other local
unions formed during the life of the
agreement, provides for the 40-hour
week, consisting Of eight hours per
day for five days for all cigar makers,
with an additional four hours on the
sixth day at the option of the employ
er. The regular h0urs of labor for
packers, strippers, selectors, banders,
trimmers, cellophaners and clerks
will be determined by immediate nego-
tiations between the parties to the
agreement.


The members of the Cigar Manu-
faeturers' Association agree to employ
only members in good standing of the
Cigar Makers International Union
with the stipulation that the union
shall at all times furnish the employ
ers with competent union help.


Wage rates under the agreement
will be determined by negotiations be-
tween representatives of the employ
ers and the union.


Under "employe representation" the
agreement provides that the union
shall have the right to be represented
by a joint advisory board composed
of workers elected by the local unions
and shop collector, elected outside
the factory premises by the workers
of each shop.


In case OF grievances, provision is
made for their settlement in each shop
with reference of unsettled grievances
to the joint advisory board and the
employer, and finally, to the duly ac-
credited officers of the Cigar Makers
international Union.


An interesting feature of the agree
ment is the statement that it is based
on the principles of collective bargain
ing as means of eliminating unneces-
sary strikes, lockouts, boycotts, and
for the stabilization of employment
"in accordance with the provisions of
the National Labor Relations Act as
construed and determined by the Su-
preme Court of the United States,"
with the added stipulation "that any
amendments, decisions of the Supreme
Court or other Qualifications of this
Act from such Supreme Court shall be
and are considered part of this agree
| ment."

present German Army is not only un-
tried, but, all expert reports agree, is
immensely inferior in numbers, arms
and training to that of 1914.


It would take more than a man and
a boy to make the Rhine fortifications
secure against the French Army. Most
of the present German reserve, also
inferior to that of the old German
Army, would be required for that job.


Germany would have 11 first-line
divisions against Czechoslovakia's
seven first line and seven second line.
And, remember, Germany could not
win with three against two on the
Western front in the World War. The
allies had more than three to two at
the finish.


If Hungary came in on the side of
Germany, it would be with seven first
line divisions. This would bring in
Rumania, with 9 divisions, and Rus-
sia might join Rumania. But, without
reckoning them in, or Britain, France
and Italy in, we stick to the prospect
of Czechoslovakia fighting the war
single.


Without the aid of Rumania's 900
planes or Russia's 1000 exclusive of
1000 in the Far East, Czechoslovakia
has 800 planes to Germany's 1000.
Prague being a transport center, it is
on the cards that German bombers
would seek to reduce it to ruins, but
not without reprisals on German
cities by Czech bombers.


Natural and Manmade Defenses.


The German Army may have the
Czech frontier in tactical wise, but it
is a strong natural frontier for de-
fenses fashioned by powerful artificial
defenses. The Germans, wherever
they concentrate, will be fighting uphill
against the Czechs, who will be shoot-
ing downhill.


For 10 years the Czech Army had
been preparing for the blow it now
faces. It has ample modern arms made
by its own Skoda works, the third
largest arms plant in Continental Eu-
rope. Supporting it are ample sup-
plies and a web of good roads for the
prompt movement of troops on an in-
terior line.


If the Czechs decide to fight after
all, they will not be the only ones
who will die. They will fight for their
own as the French fought at Verdun.

Shore Line railroad in the eighties

those travelling along the tracks but

rious authorities seem far-fetched.
One authority's distinction between
the tramp bum and hobo was: ''The
hobo works and wanders, the tramp
dreams and wanders, the bum
drinks and wanders."
